Based on the search results, here's what I found on ordinal classification in NLP with applications to sentiment analysis and essay scoring:

## Ordinal Classification in NLP

Ordinal Classification (OC) tasks involve assigning items to classes that have a relative ordering, such as positive, neutral, negative in sentiment analysis. It differs from n-ary classification by considering ordinal relationships between classes, and differs from ranking tasks because it requires category matching rather than just relative ordering.

Ordinal classification is a key task in NLP with many applications requiring ordering or ranking in the output such as Sentiment Analysis, Rating Prediction, and Age Group Classification, where output categories have a natural ordering.

## Approaches to Ordinal Classification

Ordinal classification tasks can be tackled using one of two approaches - explicit vs implicit. With Pretrained Language Models (PLMs), it became possible to tackle ordinality through the implicit semantics of the labels.

## Essay Scoring Applications

Automated essay scoring (AES) predicts multiple rubric-defined trait scores for each essay, where each trait follows an ordered discrete rating scale. Decision-Level Ordinal Modeling (DLOM) makes scoring an explicit ordinal decision by reusing the LM head to extract score-wise logits on predefined score tokens, enabling direct optimization and analysis in the score space.

I found the paper you're looking for! Here are the key details:

"Beat LLMs at Their Own Game: Zero-Shot LLM-Generated Text Detection via Querying ChatGPT" was published by Zhu et al. at the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP).

**Core Method:**
The method is based on the intuition that ChatGPT will make fewer revisions to LLM-generated texts than to human-written texts, because texts generated by LLMs are more in accord with the generation logic and statistical patterns learned by LLMs like ChatGPT. If the text to be detected and its ChatGPT-revised version have a higher degree of similarity, the text is more likely to be LLM-generated.

**Results:**
Extensive experiments on various datasets and tasks show that the method can effectively detect LLM-generated texts and has better generalization ability and is more stable across various datasets compared with other detection methods.

The code is publicly available at https://github.com/thunlp/LLM-generated-text-detection.

```text
1	To assess whether depth signal extends beyond handcrafted features, we fine-tune a pretrained language model end-to-end as a depth classifier using QLoRA \cite{qlora}.
2	
3	\paragraph{Setup.}
4	We fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B-Base with LoRA rank 16, learning rate $2 \times 10^{-4}$, and 3 epochs, framing depth estimation as 5-class sequence classification (gen-0 through gen-4).\footnote{Evaluated on the original 6-generator subset; XGBoost 3-class F1\,=\,0.789. We expect 8-generator training to further improve given additional diversity; the comparison direction is preserved.}
5	For 3-class evaluation, we collapse predictions into gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ post hoc.
6	All results use the same LOGO protocol as the main experiments.
7	
8	\begin{table}[h]
9	\centering
10	\small
11	\caption{QLoRA end-to-end depth classification vs.\ XGBoost on handcrafted features, under LOGO evaluation.}
12	\label{tab:qlora}
13	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
14	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
15	\toprule
16	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{5-class F1} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{Per-class F1 (5-class)} \\
17	\midrule
18	XGBoost (7 features) & 0.501 $\pm$ 0.038 & 0.789 & --- \\
19	QLoRA (Qwen3-0.6B)   & 0.583 $\pm$ 0.010 & 0.905 $\pm$ 0.003 & 0.999\,/\,0.796\,/\,0.413\,/\,0.259\,/\,0.447 \\
20	\bottomrule
21	\end{tabular}}
22	\end{table}
23	
24	\paragraph{Results.}
25	QLoRA achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.905 ($\pm$0.003), a +11.6\,pp improvement over the XGBoost baseline (0.789).
26	On 5-class evaluation, QLoRA reaches F1\,=\,0.583 ($\pm$0.010) vs.\ 0.501 for XGBoost (+8.2\,pp), with the largest gains at gen-1 (0.796 vs.\ 0.634) and gen-2 (0.413 vs.\ 0.268).
27	The gen-2/gen-3 boundary remains the primary failure mode (gen-3 F1\,=\,0.259), consistent with the feature-level analysis in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
28	
29	\paragraph{Hyperparameter robustness.}
30	A second run with LoRA rank 32 and seed 123 yields 5-class F1\,=\,0.587 ($\pm$0.005) and 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 ($\pm$0.004), which confirms stability across hyperparameter and seed variation ($\Delta < 1$\,pp on both metrics).
31	
32	\paragraph{Implications.}
33	The substantial 3-class improvement demonstrates that raw token embeddings contain depth signal beyond what summary statistics capture; the seven handcrafted features are a strong but lossy compression of the full distributional information.
34	End-to-end fine-tuning exploits token-level patterns (e.g., positional regularities, n-gram repetitions) that aggregate features cannot represent.
35	This confirms that the depth signal documented in our main analysis is real and exploitable beyond engineered features, while the handcrafted approach retains practical advantages: interpretability, computational efficiency (no GPU inference), and the ability to reveal the differential depth response pattern that motivates the task formulation.
36	
```

Now I have a comprehensive view. Let me analyze each candidate experiment.

### Candidate A: QLoRA Instruct

**Current state:**
- QLoRA on base models: 3-class F1 = 0.905 (vs XGBoost 0.789, +11.6pp)
- Instruct XGBoost retrain: within-model binary F1 = 0.590-0.660 (below base 0.69-0.72)
- Instruct 7-feature: DDR partition compressed (silhouette 0.632 → 0.338)


- QLoRA fine-tuning would test whether end-to-end learning can recover the depth signal that handcrafted features lose under instruction tuning, which would either validate depth classification as a real phenomenon or confirm that instruction tuning genuinely degrades this capability. The instruct results show a puzzling pattern: 3-class performance drops sharply by 3.7-19.9pp, but binary F1 stays relatively stable, suggesting the degradation isn't uniform across task complexity.

- The real test is whether QLoRA can substantially outperform XGBoost on instruct models like it does on base models (+11.6pp), though the binary-only baseline of 0.590-0.660 is already concerning and might limit how much improvement is possible. Either way, the result will clarify whether instruction tuning fundamentally alters the feature space or just makes it harder for shallow models to extract the signal.

For timing, 12-32 hours across 3-4 models is manageable with parallel GPUs, giving 4-8 hours wall time within the 6-day window. The moderate ROI means this is informative but probably won't be the deciding factor for the 3.0→3.5 jump.

On the generator-identity ablation front, I'm realizing the proposal to train on a single generator and test cross-generator is actually different from LOGO, which trains on 7 generators and holds out 1. Single-generator training would be a much stricter test of whether the depth signal generalizes across different generators.

If a classifier trained on just one generator's data still transfers to others, that's strong evidence the signal isn't tied to generator identity. If it fails, LOGO is already the right control and single-gen is just too data-starved. The cost is minimal—just XGBoost, no GPU—and even negative results would strengthen LOGO's position, so this has high ROI for addressing the reviewer's concern.

For the larger model option, getting anything over 8B to work on the RTX 5090 is tight. Quantized 13B inference might be possible but QLoRA training could hit memory limits, and generation alone would eat up significant time. The value is moderate since it fills a scale gap but probably won't shift the overall narrative much, especially when Mistral-7B already demonstrates the pattern.

So my ranking is B first, then A, then C. B is the must-do—it costs minutes and directly tackles the cross-model confound concern. A is worth considering since it addresses a real limitation, though there's real risk: if QLoRA instruct dramatically outperforms XGBoost instruct, that's valuable, but if they're similar, it's wasted effort. C should wait for the camera-ready version given the time constraints.

Looking at the instruct data more carefully, the existing Table 4 results already show strong F1 scores (0.813-0.875), which tells me the depth signal is present in those features. The real question is whether QLoRA can extract more from them, but given how compressed the instruct distributions are, there might not be much additional signal to find. The downside risk is actually limited though—even a negative result just confirms that instruct features are already squeezed. The bigger concern is the time cost: 4-8 hours of wall time plus analysis and writing probably adds up to a full day or two of work.

I should skip the larger model experiment since the limitations section already addresses that. But there's another angle worth considering: I haven't verified whether the paper includes a formal significance test comparing the LOGO binary F1 against the best individual baseline using McNemar's test. That would be a quick computation if it's missing.

Actually, looking at the results, this is already handled—the paper mentions McNemar p-values for feature group comparisons and uses paired bootstrap for baseline comparisons, so that's covered.

I'm also wondering if there's a pattern in how LOGO performs across different generators. The per-generator F1 ranges from 0.633 to 0.724, which is substantial, but the paper already discusses the Pythia same-family affinity issue and notes the cross-reference spread is only 0.013, so that's accounted for too.

The generator-identity ablation really does seem like the strongest missing experiment. Now I need to think about what would actually push this from a 3.0 to a 3.5 in terms of findings.

The jump comes down to stronger novelty, more thorough evaluation, better positioning against related work, and cleaner writing. Experiments B and the text revisions from R26 are the most direct path forward, with A as a nice-to-have if there's time. C isn't worth the risk. The real constraint is fitting everything into the 6-day window—experiments, paper revisions, and submission logistics like code packaging and the OpenReview form. Spending too much time on QLoRA instruct could eat into the submission prep.

        "content": "\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\nThe DDR tri-partition is consistent with a location/shape decomposition: under fixed temperature $\\tau$ and nucleus $p$, the softmax output distribution's shape is constrained by decoding configuration, while iterative conditioning shifts the input distribution's location.\nAn informal conjecture is that temperature acts as a shape control parameter that bounds entropy spread, so recursive conditioning can shift the mean but not escape the shape constraint imposed by $\\tau$; this would explain both high-temperature degradation and shape-feature stability.\nThis interpretation is post-hoc; formal analysis remains open.\nDDR is a parameter-dependent empirical decomposition, not a universal property of recursive generation: ablations (\\S\\ref{sec:results-differential}) show degradation at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\\,pp) and variation across prompt types.\n\nInstruction tuning fundamentally alters the depth signal across all three tested families (Appendix~\\ref{app:instruct}): entropy-mean $\\rho$ reverses sign consistently ($-0.6$ base $\\rightarrow$ $+0.23$ to $+0.48$ instruct), and retraining on instruction-tuned data partially recovers within-model binary F1 ($+$7--27\\,pp) but remains below base-model levels (0.69--0.72).\nThe DDR partition structure itself degrades ($k{=}2$ silhouette: 0.632 $\\rightarrow$ 0.338; cross-condition transfer near chance), restricting the structured partition to base models; within-model classification remains partially feasible with domain-specific retraining (Appendix~\\ref{app:instruct}).\nCross-temperature transfer degrades at $t{=}1.0$ (Appendix~\\ref{app:cross-temp}); a preliminary downstream pilot ($n{=}3$ seeds; Appendix~\\ref{app:downstream}) does not detect a depth-composition effect on training utility, though the sample size is insufficient for conclusions.\n\nThe QLoRA end-to-end classifier (3-class F1\\,=\\,0.905; Appendix~\\ref{app:qlora}) confirms richer representations capture depth signal beyond the 7-feature set; the handcrafted ensemble trades classification ceiling for the interpretability that enables DDR decomposition.\nThree classes represent the practical ceiling (5-class F1 ${\\approx}$0.50; Appendix~\\ref{app:finer-depth}), with simulated editing suggesting graceful degradation (Appendix~\\ref{app:human-edit}).\nDDR is distinct from model collapse \\cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: unlike training-loop collapse, which irreversibly erodes distributional coverage through parameter updates, inference-chain drift under fixed parameters is fully reversible and leaves distributional shape near-stationary ($d < 0.10$; variance ratios 0.98--1.12).\n",

        "totalLines": 16
      }

        "content": "% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains\n\\begin{abstract}\nText generated by large language models (LLMs) increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, producing recursive chains that progressively diverge from human-written text.\nAs such text contaminates training corpora, distinguishing generation depth from binary authorship becomes important for data provenance.\nWe study this phenomenon in base (pretrained) models and ask whether the drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as \\emph{generation depth classification} (gen-0\\,/\\,gen-1\\,/\\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).\nAcross eight base models from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we identify a \\emph{differential depth response} (DDR): features partition into drifting, intermediate, and near-stationary groups, consistent with recursive generation shifting the negative log-likelihood (NLL) location under a reference model while distributional shape remains stable.\nA 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\\,=\\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, generalizing across model families.\nThe depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, restricting current applicability to base models.\n\\end{abstract}\n",
        "numLines": 10,
        "startLine": 1,
        "totalLines": 10
      }
    },
    "displayPath": "../../../artifacts/_project/paper/abstract.tex"

1	% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
2	\begin{abstract}
3	Text generated by large language models (LLMs) increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, producing recursive chains that progressively diverge from human-written text.
4	As such text contaminates training corpora, distinguishing generation depth from binary authorship becomes important for data provenance.
5	We study this phenomenon in base (pretrained) models and ask whether the drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as \emph{generation depth classification} (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).
6	Across eight base models from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we identify a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): features partition into drifting, intermediate, and near-stationary groups, consistent with recursive generation shifting the negative log-likelihood (NLL) location under a reference model while distributional shape remains stable.
7	A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, generalizing across model families.
8	The depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, restricting current applicability to base models.
9	\end{abstract}
10

      "content": "% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains\n\\begin{abstract}\nText generated by large language models (LLMs) increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, producing recursive chains that progressively diverge from human-written text.\nAs such text contaminates training corpora, distinguishing generation depth from binary authorship becomes important for data provenance.\nWe study this phenomenon in base (pretrained) models and ask whether the drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as \\emph{generation depth classification} (gen-0\\,/\\,gen-1\\,/\\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).\nAcross eight base models from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we identify a \\emph{differential depth response} (DDR): features partition into drifting, intermediate, and near-stationary groups, consistent with recursive generation shifting the negative log-likelihood (NLL) location under a reference model while distributional shape remains stable.\nA 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\\,=\\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, generalizing across model families.\nThe depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, restricting current applicability to base models.\n\\end{abstract}\n",
      "numLines": 10,
